title: Tenanted Routing Runtime Patterns and Contract-aware Controls
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note collects pragmatic runtime patterns for tenant/org-aware routing that are explicitly contract-SLA conscious and designed for multi-region deployments. Goal: enable predictable latency and cost isolation across tiers while keeping cheap fallbacks for degraded capacity. This is intentionally operational: small, testable primitives + a control-plane mapping to contract terms.

Executive summary:
- Treat 'customer contract' as first-class routing input. A contract maps to: tier (gold/silver/bronze), contract SLAs (p99 latency SLO, throughput minimum, availability), quota/billing profile, and permitted fallback models/regions.
- Split decision plane into two layers: policy-evaluator (fast, stateless) and policy-orchestrator (slow, eventual, authoritative).
- Implement per-tenant micro-budgets (short window) and debt accounting. Allow borrowing within limits for bursty workloads from pooled capacity with automatic reconciliation.
- Noisy neighbor defenses: adaptive shedder + soft-penalty token-bucket + escalation to per-org throttling or route-isolation.

Key concepts and primitives:
1) Policy token (immutable per-request): {tenant_id, contract_id, tier, region_hint, trace_id} — used by runtime for routing decisions and observability.
2) Fast policy-evaluator (FE): in-proc, O(1) lookup: tenant->routing-key, tier->priority, quota-window->remaining. FE gets lightweight updates via push from control-plane caches. FE must be able to operate for 30s of disconnected operation.
3) Policy-orchestrator (PO): central control-plane service that owns the authoritative map: contract->routing policy, throttles, allowed-models, multi-region failover preferences. PO exposes: preview API, bulk update, and history (auditable).
4) Routing keys: (primary_region, fallback_region_set, class_of_service) — used to select candidate endpoints.
5) Quota primitives: short-window token-buckets (per-tenant-per-route), long-window consumption ledger (billing & alerts), and soft-budgets for cache/burst borrowing.

Routing decision flow (per-request):
- Enrich request with policy token (auth layer consults PO cache).
- FE computes candidate endpoints ordered by: (1) SLA-compatibility, (2) latency-cost tradeoff, (3) regional affinity, (4) capacity headroom.
- If FE finds candidate in primary region with sufficient headroom -> route.
- If not, consult configured fallback sequence: pinned alternative model in another region, cheaper model in same region, or queued/batched delayed execution depending on SLA tolerance.

Noisy-neighbor controls (practical patterns):
- Soft-penalty stage: apply increased per-token cost accounting to offending tenant (metering flag). This is reversible and visible in billing logs.
- Reactive shedder: when host-level load > threshold, run randomized drop weighted by tenant priority; use deterministic hashing to keep drops consistent per-tenant for debugging.
- Isolation escalation: move tenant to dedicated pool or isolated cgroup when observed violation exceeds configured thresholds for X minutes. Trigger is a combination of fault injection tolerant signals: sustained CPU/GPU stall, KV cache thrash, or network egress spikes.
- Cooperative backpressure: clients can opt into cheaper approximation models or partial responses (e.g., truncate context) in exchange for better SLA standing. Provide ECD (early-consent-degradation) hooks in API to mark such requests.

Quota and debt model details:
- Short-window token bucket (W=15s): refill_rate = tier_base_rate * contract_multiplier. Allows intra-second smoothing and burst headroom.
- Debt ledger: when bucket exhausted, allow negative tokens up to debt_limit (based on contract credit). Debt is reconciled by background jobs that throttle further borrowing and create billing adjustments.
- Emergency salvage: if global capacity constrained, PO can flip global policy to ‘debt-free mode’ where no borrowing allowed; FE must then enforce strict rejection for debtors.

SLA mapping and verification:
- Each route has an SLA profile: target p50/p95/p99, cost-weight, and allowed fallbacks.
- Periodic verification job: sample requests end-to-end with injected headers to validate that fallback behavior abides by contract (e.g., gold customers never hit model X fallback more than 1% monthly).
- Regression alerts: integrate Redwood Optimize evals to detect quality regressions when fallback model used.

Multi-region considerations:
- Affinity window: prefer primary region for latency; allow up to N cross-region hops/day per tenant (contract-controlled). Track cross-region egress for billing and privacy (some contracts may forbid cross-region).
- Geo isolation: PO stores region_allowed flag per-contract. FE must honor this even if capacity would benefit from cross-region routing.
- Fast failover vs. gradual: for critical tiers, failover should be fast (circuit-break to fallback region). For lower tiers, prefer queued retry with jitter.

Observability and tooling:
- Emit per-request policy_token and routing_decision events to tracing/metrics. Key metrics: tenant_p99_latency_by_route, tenant_quota_usage_short_window, tenant_debt, tenant_fallback_rate, noisy_neighbor_incidents.
- Dashboards: per-contract SLO panel, global capacity map, hot-tenant list.
- Debugging: ability to replay a tenant’s request history through simulated FE with proposed policy changes. PO exposes dry-run endpoints.

Operational playbooks (short):
- If primary region sees >10% SLA violations for gold: enable transient priority-preemption (safest routes get preempted), notify SRE, and spin up standby pools in fallbacks.
- On noisy tenant detection: mark soft-penalty -> wait 5m -> if persists, enforce hard throttle and open ticket to SE for reaching out.

Open questions and experiments to run:
- Optimal debt_limit vs. churn: how much borrowing materially increases tail latency? Need sim.
- Effectiveness of deterministic randomized shedding vs. strictly priority-based drop.
- Economics: price-of-fallback (cost delta) billing patterns that encourage sensible client behavior.

Next steps (concrete):
1) Small spike experiment: implement FE cache shim with token-bucket + debt simulation behind feature flag for 2% of traffic. (Owner: Ethan)
2) PO API: add contract->region_allowed and contract->debt_limit fields; expose dry-run. (Owner: Priya)
3) Create SLO verification job and dashboard (Owner: Dmitri)

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc focuses on runtime-level controls rather than product-level entitlement UI. We assume product team will generate contract artifacts that PO consumes.
- Keep control-plane data model minimal: prefer composable small fields over large monolithic blobs.

Appendix: quick pseudocode for FE routing decision:
  function route_request(req):
    token = enrich_with_policy(req.auth_token)
    bucket = get_bucket(token.tenant_id, token.route)
    if bucket.tokens > 0 or within_debt_allowed(token):
      endpoints = rank_candidates(token)
      return pick_best(endpoints)
    else:
      if token.tier == 'gold': return queue_or_proxy(req)
      else: return reject_with_backoff(err_code=429)

-- end of note --
